title: DNA replication
introduction: How can a cell preserve its genetic sequence while synthesizing two new DNA duplexes, and how do polymerases overcome antiparallel templates?

sections.guidingQuestion: What must happen before two daughter cells inherit complete copies of a chromosome?
sections.explanation:
Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. Accurate sequence copying allows the new cells in a growing root, a healing wound or a dividing bacterium to retain the genetic instructions of the parent cell. It does not mean that replication is perfectly error-free; rare mistakes can persist as mutations.

The DNA sequence serves as an ordered template. Replication copies the whole DNA molecule; transcription later uses selected DNA regions to produce RNA. Keeping these processes distinct explains how a cell can preserve genes while changing which genes it expresses.

Follow the consequence: an unreplicated chromosome contains one DNA double helix; a correctly replicated chromosome contains two identical sister chromatids. Copying sequence information first makes it possible for division to supply each future daughter nucleus with the same instructions. In an ordinary cell cycle this copying occurs during S phase, before mitosis—not during cytokinesis.
sections.revisionSummary: DNA replication copies genetic information before growth, cell division and reproduction. In eukaryotic cells it occurs before mitosis so daughter cells can inherit the same DNA sequence.
terms: DNA replication: synthesis of new DNA with the same base sequence as the template
Chromosome: DNA molecule with associated proteins that carries genetic information
sections.workedExample: A skin basal cell duplicates its genomic DNA before mitosis so its daughters can continue producing skin tissue.

sections.guidingQuestion: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?
sections.explanation:
The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive.

A pairs with T and G with C. Each exposed parental base therefore helps select the corresponding nucleotide for the new strand. DNA polymerase also contributes to accuracy through nucleotide selection and, where present, proofreading; complementary base pairing by itself does not make replication infallible.
sections.revisionSummary: Each parental DNA strand templates a new complementary strand. Both daughter double helices therefore contain one old and one new strand; complementary base pairing helps preserve sequence accuracy.
terms: Semi-conservative replication: each daughter DNA double helix contains one parental strand and one newly made strand
Complementary base pairing: A pairs with T and G with C in DNA

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?
sections.explanation:
Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands. The sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact at the fork; helicase does not cut the strands into nucleotides.

DNA polymerase reads an exposed template and joins complementary deoxyribonucleotides by forming phosphodiester bonds in the growing daughter strand. In cellular replication it extends a pre-existing 3′ end rather than starting synthesis from nothing. Helicase separates the strands; polymerase builds their complementary copies.
sections.revisionSummary: Helicase exposes the two parental templates by disrupting hydrogen bonds. DNA polymerase selects complementary DNA nucleotides and links them into new strands by phosphodiester bonds.
terms: Helicase: enzyme that unwinds DNA and separates paired strands by disrupting hydrogen bonds
DNA polymerase: enzyme that adds DNA nucleotides to a growing complementary strand
sections.workedExample: At an advancing bacterial replication fork, helicase opens the duplex while polymerase synthesizes DNA along each exposed template.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which sequence of conditions describes one ordinary PCR cycle?
sections.explanation:
A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome.

DNA has a negatively charged sugar–phosphate backbone, so an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. In an appropriate gel, shorter DNA fragments generally travel farther than longer ones. Compare bands against a DNA ladder to estimate length; a matching band position does not reveal the fragment's complete base sequence.
sections.revisionSummary: PCR amplifies a chosen DNA segment using strand separation, primer annealing and Taq-polymerase extension. Gel electrophoresis separates the negatively charged fragments, with smaller pieces generally travelling farther.
terms: PCR (polymerase chain reaction): repeated temperature cycles that amplify a selected DNA region
Primer: short DNA sequence that binds a template and provides a starting point for polymerase
Gel electrophoresis: separation of DNA fragments by migration through a gel toward the positive electrode
sections.workedExample: Amplify a candidate 300-base-pair locus with paired primers, then compare its gel band position with a DNA ladder.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are several independent DNA markers used in forensic profiling?
sections.explanation:
Forensic investigations and parentage testing compare informative DNA markers. Amplification makes small samples analysable and gel or capillary separation distinguishes fragment-length patterns. Agreement at one marker is weak evidence; combining multiple independent markers can greatly reduce the chance of a coincidental match.

A DNA-marker match is evidence that two samples may share a source, not certainty about identity. Multiple independent markers reduce coincidental matches, but contamination, close relatives, population frequencies and sample handling still matter to a forensic or parentage conclusion.
sections.revisionSummary: PCR and fragment separation support forensic and parentage comparisons. More independent markers make an accidental profile match less likely, but interpretation still depends on sample quality, controls and statistics.
terms: DNA profile: pattern of DNA markers used to compare biological samples
Genetic marker: detectable DNA region that differs among individuals
False match: apparent agreement between samples that do not have the same source
sections.workedExample: A disputed parentage case compares several inherited short tandem repeat markers, rather than relying on a single PCR band.

misconceptions.misconception: One matching DNA band establishes the donor's identity with certainty.
misconceptions.correction: A reliable identification integrates multiple markers, controls and statistical interpretation.

sections.guidingQuestion: At which end can DNA polymerase add the next nucleotide?
sections.explanation:
A DNA strand has chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends because nucleotides have a phosphate-linked 5′ carbon and a hydroxyl-bearing 3′ carbon. The two template strands in a duplex run antiparallel. DNA polymerase attaches an incoming nucleotide's 5′ phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the growing strand; every new DNA strand therefore elongates 5′→3′.

DNA polymerase bonds the incoming nucleotide's 5′ phosphate to the free 3′-OH of the growing strand. Every daughter DNA strand therefore extends 5′→3′, with its template read antiparallel, 3′→5′. A replication-fork arrow and a strand-synthesis arrow describe different directions.
sections.revisionSummary: DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the growing strand's 3′-OH, so every new DNA strand extends 5′→3′ while its template is read 3′→5′.
terms: 5′ end: end of a DNA strand with a phosphate associated with sugar carbon 5′
3′ end: end with the sugar's free 3′ hydroxyl group (–OH)
Antiparallel: the two DNA strands run in opposite 5′→3′ directions
sections.workedExample: For template 3′-ACGT-5′ read from left to right, polymerase extends 5′-TGCA-3′ toward the right.

misconceptions.correction: Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes the newly synthesized lagging strand from the leading strand?
sections.explanation:
On the leading-strand template, a newly primed strand is extended continuously in the same overall direction in which the replication fork opens. Because the polymerase can only extend a 3′ end, the leading template is read 3′→5′ toward the fork.

The opposite template polarity requires repeated RNA primers on the lagging strand. Each Okazaki fragment still grows 5′→3′, but away from the advancing fork; the RNA primers are later replaced and ligase joins the fragments. The leading strand instead grows continuously toward the fork after its initial primer.
sections.revisionSummary: Because polymerase can extend DNA only 5′→3′, the leading strand is made continuously toward the fork, while the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments that are later joined.
terms: Leading strand: daughter strand synthesized continuously toward the advancing replication fork
Lagging strand: daughter strand synthesized discontinuously away from the fork
Okazaki fragment: short DNA segment made from a new primer on the lagging strand
sections.workedExample: At a right-moving fork, an individual Okazaki fragment begins nearer the fork and grows to the left; the leading daughter grows to the right.

misconceptions.correction: Okazaki fragments are individually synthesized 5′→3′, but in the direction opposite fork travel.

sections.guidingQuestion: In bacterial DNA replication, which enzyme mainly extends new DNA from RNA primers?
sections.explanation:
In the prokaryotic system specified by the guide, primase makes short RNA primers that provide the free 3′ end needed by DNA polymerase III. Polymerase III extends the DNA segment while reading the parental template. Leading synthesis typically needs one initiation at a fork; lagging synthesis needs a fresh primer for each fragment.

DNA polymerase I removes the temporary RNA primers and replaces those nucleotides with DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone. Primase, polymerase III, polymerase I and ligase have distinct roles in this prokaryotic model.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which activity directly removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide during bacterial polymerase III proofreading?
sections.explanation:
Bacterial DNA polymerase III tests the terminal base pair while the daughter strand is being extended. If the 3′ end carries an incorrectly matched nucleotide, its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity removes that terminal nucleotide and the polymerase incorporates the properly matched replacement.

A mismatch at the newly added 3′ end can cause bacterial DNA polymerase III to pause. Its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity removes the incorrect terminal nucleotide, allowing a correctly paired nucleotide to be added. Other DNA-repair systems act separately; proofreading greatly reduces, but does not eliminate, replication errors.

questions.prompt: A cell enters mitosis without duplicating its chromosomal DNA, although it has synthesized many proteins. Which process was missing for both daughter cells to receive complete copies of the chromosomes?

options.feedback: DNA replication produces two copies of each chromosome's sequence; subsequent chromosome segregation can then distribute one copy to each daughter cell.

options.text: Translation of every mRNA into protein
options.feedback: Translation uses ribosomes to make proteins from mRNA. Making proteins does not copy the DNA sequences that daughter cells inherit.

options.text: Breaking every phosphodiester bond in each chromosome
options.feedback: Phosphodiester bonds form the sugar–phosphate backbone. Replication separates base-paired strands without destroying the entire DNA backbone.

options.text: Replacing thymine in DNA with uracil
options.feedback: Uracil is ordinarily found in RNA; DNA replication preserves complementary DNA base pairing (A–T, C–G) rather than converting DNA to RNA.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain replication in DNA replication and correct this claim: "Replication makes RNA copies for translation."
questions.answer: Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. Accurate sequence copying allows the new cells in a growing root, a healing wound or a dividing bacterium to retain the genetic instructions of the parent cell. It does not mean that replication is perfectly error-free; rare mistakes can persist as mutations. Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA. A skin basal cell duplicates its genomic DNA before mitosis so its daughters can continue producing skin tissue.
markingPoints: Follow the consequence: an unreplicated chromosome contains one DNA double helix; a correctly replicated chromosome contains two identical sister chromatids
Copying sequence information first makes it possible for division to supply each future daughter nucleus with the same instructions
Correct the common inference: Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA.

questions.prompt: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?

options.text: One parental and one new strand
options.feedback: Each original strand templates a new complementary strand, so each daughter DNA duplex contains one parental and one newly synthesized strand.
Keeping both parental strands together in one duplex describes the conservative model, not semiconservative replication.
Daughter DNA is related to the parental molecule by complementary base pairing; new strands are not random unrelated molecules.
Each daughter duplex retains one original template strand; a duplex containing only new strands is not the semiconservative outcome.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain semi-conservative in DNA replication and correct this claim: "One daughter duplex receives both original DNA strands."
questions.answer: The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive. Each daughter duplex contains one original and one newly synthesized strand. For a short template 3′-TACG-5′, the new antiparallel DNA strand is 5′-ATGC-3′.
markingPoints: A template strand does not dictate where its own bases remain; it determines the order of incoming complementary nucleotides
Separating the two parental strands therefore produces two templates, each leading to one parental-plus-new double helix
Correct the common inference: Each daughter duplex contains one original and one newly synthesized strand.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?

options.text: Separate DNA strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds
options.feedback: Helicase unwinds the parental duplex by disrupting hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; covalent sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact.

options.text: Join Okazaki fragments by covalent bonds
options.feedback: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone between Okazaki fragments; helicase unwinds double-stranded DNA.
Ribosomes join amino acids during protein synthesis; helicase acts on DNA base pairs, not peptide formation.
RNA primer removal and replacement involve nucleases and DNA polymerase, not helicase's strand-separation function.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain helicase in DNA replication and correct this claim: "Helicase breaks covalent bonds in the DNA backbone."
questions.answer: Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands. The sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact at the fork; helicase does not cut the strands into nucleotides. Helicase separates strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds, leaving both backbones intact. At an advancing bacterial replication fork, helicase opens the duplex while polymerase synthesizes DNA along each exposed template.
markingPoints: Helicase disrupts hydrogen bonds between paired bases without cutting the sugar–phosphate backbone
Exposed parental strands are templates; DNA polymerase selects matching DNA nucleotides and makes covalent phosphodiester links in the growing daughter chain
Correct the common inference: Helicase separates strands by disrupting base-pair hydrogen bonds, leaving both backbones intact.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of conditions describes one ordinary PCR cycle?

options.feedback: Correct. A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers.
Consider why “Translation, transcription, replication” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.
Consider why “Polymerase extension, protein folding, mitosis” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.
Consider why “Gel separation, ligation, protein sorting” does not answer this question. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain pcr in DNA replication and correct this claim: "DNA moves to the negative electrode in ordinary gel electrophoresis."
questions.answer: A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome. DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode. Amplify a candidate 300-base-pair locus with paired primers, then compare its gel band position with a DNA ladder.
markingPoints: Temperature makes three different things possible in successive PCR stages: high heat separates template strands, cooling allows short primers to anneal to flanking complementary sites, and extension at the polymerase's working temperature copies the bounded region
Taq polymerase is heat-stable
Correct the common inference: DNA has a negatively charged backbone and migrates toward the positive electrode.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain genetic marker in DNA replication and correct this claim: "One matching DNA band establishes the donor's identity with certainty."
questions.answer: Forensic investigations and parentage testing compare informative DNA markers. Amplification makes small samples analysable and gel or capillary separation distinguishes fragment-length patterns. Agreement at one marker is weak evidence; combining multiple independent markers can greatly reduce the chance of a coincidental match. A reliable identification integrates multiple markers, controls and statistical interpretation. A disputed parentage case compares several inherited short tandem repeat markers, rather than relying on a single PCR band.
markingPoints: A matching DNA-band or STR profile is evidence of consistency with a sample source, not a proof that excludes contamination, relatives or procedural error
More independently selected markers usually decrease the probability of a coincidental match
Correct the common inference: A reliable identification integrates multiple markers, controls and statistical interpretation.

options.text: The free 3′ end of the growing strand

options.text: The 5′ end of the growing strand

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain 5′ end in DNA replication and correct this claim: "DNA polymerase sometimes builds new DNA 3′→5′ on the lagging strand."
questions.answer: A DNA strand has chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends because nucleotides have a phosphate-linked 5′ carbon and a hydroxyl-bearing 3′ carbon. The two template strands in a duplex run antiparallel. DNA polymerase attaches an incoming nucleotide's 5′ phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the growing strand; every new DNA strand therefore elongates 5′→3′. Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′. For template 3′-ACGT-5′ read from left to right, polymerase extends 5′-TGCA-3′ toward the right.
markingPoints: The phosphate of an incoming dNTP attaches to the free 3′-OH of the nascent chain, so elongation is always 5′→3′
Polymerase reads its template antiparallel, 3′→5′
Correct the common inference: Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

Okazaki fragments are eventually joined into a continuous daughter molecule
Correct the common inference: Okazaki fragments are individually synthesized 5′→3′, but in the direction opposite fork travel.

questions.prompt: An idealized PCR model begins with 20 amplifiable target duplexes and assumes perfect doubling per cycle. Calculate the expected count after four cycles, then explain why a real reaction may produce fewer copies.
questions.answer: 20 × 2⁴ = 320 target duplexes in this idealized model. Actual reaction efficiency can be reduced by reagent limitations, incomplete primer annealing or inhibition; amplification will not always double perfectly.
